questions.question: What is the defining condition for a sequence $(\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ to be Cauchy in a metric space $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$?
options: For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there is $N \geq 1$ such that $d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k) \gt \varepsilon$ for all $j,k\geq N$.
For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there is $N \geq 1$ such that $d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k) \lt \varepsilon$ for all $j,k\geq N$.
There is one fixed $N$ that works for every metric space.
Every term of the sequence must be equal to the first term.

questions.question: In the metric-space definition of a Cauchy sequence, what replaces the absolute value used for real sequences?
options: The metric $d$
The index $N$
The set $\boldsymbol{X}$ itself
The number $1$

questions.question: After choosing $\varepsilon = 0.1$, what is the Cauchy condition?
options: There exists $N \geq 1$ such that $d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k) \lt 0.1$ for all $j,k\geq N$.
There exists $N \geq 1$ such that $d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k) \gt 0.1$ for all $j,k\geq N$.
For all $j,k \lt N$, $d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k) \lt 0.1$.
The first term must satisfy $d(\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_1) = 0.1$.

questions.question: If $(\boldsymbol{x}_n)$ converges in a metric space, what can be concluded about $(\boldsymbol{x}_n)$?
options: It is Cauchy.
It cannot be Cauchy.
It is Cauchy only if the limit is the first term.
It is Cauchy only when the metric is Euclidean.

questions.question: For a Cauchy sequence, what must happen to $d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k)$ when both $j$ and $k$ are sufficiently large?
options: It must be larger than every prescribed $\varepsilon \gt 0$.
It must equal $1$ for all large indices.
It must be smaller than any prescribed $\varepsilon \gt 0$.
It must be undefined.

questions.question: Which hidden assumption would make the statement “every Cauchy sequence converges” valid for a particular metric space?
options: The metric space has no sequences.
The metric space is complete.
The metric is never zero.
The sequence has no tail.

questions.question: Which statement best separates Cauchy behaviour from convergence?
options: Cauchy compares each term with $\boldsymbol{x}_1$; convergence uses a limit.
Convergence compares late terms; Cauchy uses a limit.
Cauchy compares early terms; convergence uses late terms only.
Cauchy compares late terms; convergence uses a limit.

questions.question: Suppose a sequence in $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$ is Cauchy but does not converge in $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$. Which conclusion is consistent?
options: The sequence cannot have any of its terms in $\boldsymbol{X}$.
The sequence must be eventually constant.
The metric $d$ is not being used.
It may cluster around a point outside $\boldsymbol{X}$.

questions.question: For $a_n=\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^n$ in $(\mathbb{Q},d)$, what does this example demonstrate?
options: Cauchy does not by itself guarantee convergence inside the space.
Its terms leave $\mathbb{Q}$, since $(1+\frac{1}{n})^n$ is irrational for large $n$.
Every Cauchy sequence in $(\mathbb{Q},d)$ converges to a point in $(\mathbb{Q},d)$.
It does not converge in $\mathbb{R}$ either, so it is not a Cauchy sequence at all.

questions.question: What must happen to $d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k)$ in a Cauchy sequence?
options: It must equal $0$ for all $j,k$.
It is below any $\varepsilon \gt 0$ for large enough $j,k$.
It must grow without bound.
It must be computed only from the first two terms.

questions.question: What replaces absolute value in the metric-space version of the Cauchy condition?
options: The scalar product only
The real part
The metric $d$
The complex conjugate

questions.question: If a sequence converges in a metric space, what can be concluded?
options: It is Cauchy.
It is not Cauchy.
It has no tail terms.
It leaves the metric space.

questions.question: Why can a Cauchy sequence fail to converge in its metric space?
options: Its terms must be infinitely far apart.
Every metric space excludes all Cauchy sequences by definition.
Its limiting point may be missing from the space.
Cauchy sequences are never bounded.

questions.question: A sequence in $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$ is Cauchy but has no limit in $\boldsymbol{X}$. Which statement is consistent with the definition?
options: Its tail terms still become arbitrarily close to each other.
Its tail terms must stay at distance at least $1$ apart.
It cannot be Cauchy by definition.
It must eventually leave $\boldsymbol{X}$ under the stated limiting assumptions.
